title: Continuum, evening of 13 October 2026: Continuum's own arcade emulator, first version
why: Arcade games have been out of the app since 12 October, when the owner removed the two arcade emulators with non-commercial licences (FinalBurn Neo and MAME 2003-Plus). Their decision: no outside arcade core, ever; arcade comes back only when Continuum has an arcade emulator of its own, the way cBoy is its own Game Boy emulator. Arcade games players already imported are still in their library, and opening one shows: "Arcade games aren't playable right now. We're building our own arcade emulator." This job is that emulator. It is a whole new emulator written from scratch, so tonight is its first version, done properly, not all of arcade history.
read_first: /projects/sandbox/.scratch/arcade-work/.kiro/steering/owner-rules.md (the 'Licences' and 'Arcade: NO MAME, no stand-in' paragraphs)
/projects/sandbox/.scratch/arcade-work/cores/continuum-gb/Cargo.toml and cores/continuum-gb/src/libretro.rs (cBoy: the pattern to copy for a standalone pure-Rust libretro core crate)
ORDERS_CHANGED_NO_DEADLINE: CANCELLED by the owner at 4 PM on 13 October: the 7:30 PM Eastern deadline your prompt mentions, and every 'if time allows' on this list. There is NO deadline and NO cutoff. Do not watch the clock, do not stop early, and do not leave anything out or cut anything short to save time. Every item on this list is required and gets finished properly: the Z80, the Pac-Man board, the app wiring, the Galaxian family and the Donkey Kong board. A board is switched on in the app once it is proven; that is how the work is done, never a reason to leave a board out. The orchestrator starts the build when all three of tonight's jobs are finished.
hard_rules: Work ONLY in /projects/sandbox/.scratch/arcade-work. Two other agents are working on the same repository right now: one on cBoy in /projects/sandbox/.scratch/cboy-work (owns cores/continuum-gb/** and .kiro/notes/docs/CBOY_*.md: never touch them), one on the engine and app in /projects/sandbox/Continuum- (two-phone link, Mesen 2 for SNES, Sega CD, 32X).

You own: cores/continuum-arcade/** (new), .kiro/notes/docs/ARCADE_CORE.md (new), and the small wiring edits that put the arcade core in the app: its own marked region in scripts/build-core.sh (follow the `# recipe-start:` / `# recipe-end:` rules that commit 393f12c introduced, and run scripts/check-core-cache.sh), native/ios/project.yml (embed it the way cBoy is embedded), native/ios/build-engine.sh if cBoy appears there, .github/workflows/ios.yml (ONLY: run the arcade crate's tests in the `checks` job next to cBoy's, and add cores/continuum-arcade/** to the push paths), and the arcade system's wiring in crates/emulator-bridge and native/ios (routing arcade games to the new core, its registry entry, the line a player sees). Do NOT edit STATUS.md, TESTING.md or HANDOFF.md tonight: the orchestrator writes those at the end.

Shared files (registry, settings screen, build-core.sh, project.yml) may be edited by the engine agent too: keep your edits small and in your own lines, and when `git pull --rebase` conflicts, keep BOTH sides, then re-run the checks before pushing.

Push straight to master. No branches, no pull requests, ever. EVERY commit message ends with [skip ci]. Push after every finished item: stage your files by name, commit, `git pull --rebase origin master && git push origin master`, retry if rejected. Never leave finished work only in the sandbox.

NEVER download, fetch or commit a commercial arcade ROM, not even for a test. Test with CPU test suites, test programs you write and assemble yourself, and openly licensed homebrew only, fetched into scratch and never committed.

Our own code, GPL-3.0-only like cBoy. Read hardware documentation and how proven emulators (MAME above all) model each board, and implement that in Continuum's own Rust; do not copy their code. A short comment per piece naming the hardware behaviour it reproduces.

The iOS build must not be able to fail because of this: build the arcade core the same OPTIONAL way cBoy is built, so if it fails to compile the .ipa ships without it and arcade games keep their current line. Pure Rust, no C dependencies, the same crate settings as cBoy.

Green before every push: `cargo test --release` in cores/continuum-arcade, plus, whenever you touch the app's wiring, `cargo test --workspace --features emulator-bridge/native-core`, `cargo clippy --workspace --features emulator-bridge/native-core`, `swiftc -frontend -parse` on changed Swift files and `bash scripts/check-core-cache.sh`. Set CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=3.
Anything a player reads is short, casual and plain. Never crash on an arcade game the core can't play, and never ask 'Which system?' for one.
per_iteration: 1. Read this file, including ORDERS_CHANGED_NO_DEADLINE. Pick the first item with done=false.
2. Read before changing: the hardware behaviour, and the app code you are wiring into.
3. Implement it with tests. Run the checks. Fix anything you broke.
5. Set done=true with a one-sentence plain-English 'result'. If every item is done, set the top-level "complete": true.

items.title: The plan, short (30 minutes at most)
items.detail: Write .kiro/notes/docs/ARCADE_CORE.md: the working name shown in the app ('cArcade', matching cBoy; the owner can rename it); the crate (cores/continuum-arcade, crate continuum_arcade, a standalone libretro core like cores/continuum-gb); how a game is recognised (arcade games are zips named after the game, like pacman.zip: read each file's name, size and CRC32 from the zip's own directory, match against a built-in list of the sets the core knows, accept merged, split and non-merged sets, and find a clone's parent zip next to it in the same folder); one module per board; the order of boards below; how each is proved; and EVERY place the app wires in a core and the arcade system, found by reading. Starting points: cBoy appears in crates/emulator-bridge/src/core_updates.rs, cores/diagnostic.rs, cores/native_core.rs, gfx/screen_layout.rs, battery_layout.rs, bridge.rs, tests/cboy_frontend.rs, native/ios/SettingsScreen.swift, build-engine.sh, ContinuumApp.swift, project.yml, scripts/extract-core-option-keys.sh, scripts/build-core.sh, scripts/check-core-cache.sh and .github/workflows/ios.yml; the arcade system appears in crates/emulator-bridge/src/achievements/console.rs, gfx/renderer.rs, import/detect.rs, import/mod.rs, import/saves.rs, uniffi_import.rs and native/ios GameArtwork.swift, ImportCenter.swift, SkinLibrary.swift, TouchControls.swift, CloudSync.swift and ContinuumApp.swift. No code in this item.
items.result: .kiro/notes/docs/ARCADE_CORE.md (pushed as 60b5b06) sets the plan: cArcade as the working name, the cores/continuum-arcade crate, how a zip set is recognised by CRC32 including merged, split and non-merged sets and a clone's parent beside it, one module per board in the order Z80, Pac-Man, app wiring, Galaxian, Donkey Kong, how each is proved against a locally built MAME with our own test programs, and every place the app wires it in - including that the first build with it rebuilds every core once, because a new core's lines sit in the shared part of build-core.sh by design.

cArcade's own Z80 is in cores/continuum-arcade (pushed as c869098): every one of SingleStepTests' 1,604,000 cases passes on every register, flag, MEMPTR, memory byte, bus access and T-state count, ZEXDOC and ZEXALL pass all 67 groups each, unit tests cover interrupt modes 0-2, the NMI, HALT and the refresh register, and the suites are fetched by scripts/fetch-test-suites.sh (checked by sha256, never committed) and say SKIPPED when absent.
items.title: The Z80 processor, proven
items.detail: Most classic arcade boards run on the Z80. Write it in Rust: every documented and undocumented instruction, the flags including the two undocumented bits, the hidden WZ/MEMPTR register those bits leak, the refresh register, interrupt modes 0, 1 and 2, NMI, HALT, the block instructions, and cycle counts. Prove it with SingleStepTests' Z80 suite (MIT-licensed JSON, one file per opcode, fetched into scratch by a script, never committed: every case must pass) and with ZEXDOC and ZEXALL run through a tiny CP/M stand-in inside the test harness. Gate both in `cargo test --release` the way cBoy gates its test ROMs (skip cleanly when the download is not there).

items.result: The Pac-Man board is in cores/continuum-arcade (pushed as 9c39306): Puck Man and Pac-Man's plain board, Pac-Man Plus's decoder, Ms. Pac-Man's daughterboard and the bootleg boards with ROM at 8000h, with the upright picture, colours, Namco sound, inputs, DIP switches, interrupt and watchdog, and nine test programs of our own match MAME 0.289 on all 1,400 frames, pixel for pixel and sound sample for sample (tests/pacman_mame.rs live, tests/pacman_board.rs against MAME's recorded hashes everywhere).
items.title: The Pac-Man board
items.detail: Namco's Pac-Man hardware: Pac-Man, Puck Man, Ms. Pac-Man (including the way its daughterboard rearranges and patches the program ROMs), Pac-Man Plus (its program and graphics decoding), and the common clones and bootlegs on the same board. The tile and sprite picture with its unusual screen layout, the colour PROMs, the Namco sound chip (three voices playing 32-step waveforms from the sound PROM), the inputs (coin, start, a four-way joystick), the DIP switches (lives, bonus life, difficulty, cocktail or upright), the watchdog, the interrupt vector the game writes to port 0, and the board's real frame rate. The picture comes out upright, the way the cabinet shows it. Prove it without commercial ROMs: write small test programs for this board yourself (an assembler built from source in scratch), and compare our picture and sound against MAME's for the same programs, with MAME built locally from source as a small subset containing only the drivers you need, in scratch, never committed (use -j3 so the other agents keep running). Pin the comparisons as tests.

items.result: Arcade games open on cArcade (pushed as 5848928): it recognises 65 Pac-Man-board sets by their chips (full, split or merged zips, a clone's parent found next to it), its DIP switches are settings with the factory defaults MAME has, Select is the coin and Start is start, save states and Restart work, a zip it can't play gets one plain line, and our own test programs played through its libretro entry points and through the app's engine match MAME frame for frame; a build without it keeps the old line, adding it rebuilds no other emulator, and the two ios.yml lines are parked in .kiro/notes/docs/ARCADE_CORE.md.
items.title: In the app: arcade games open on cArcade
items.detail: The libretro core around the boards (load a zip set, the built-in set list with names and titles, DIP switches as core options with plain labels, coin and start on the controls, the upright picture and its aspect, save states that round-trip exactly, the right frame rate), and the app's wiring from I1: arcade games route to it; a set it knows opens and plays; a set it doesn't know opens to one plain line naming the kind of games it plays now (for example: "Our arcade emulator can't play this one yet. Right now it plays Pac-Man, Ms. Pac-Man and games on the same board."), never a crash and never 'Which system?'; and the old "Arcade games aren't playable right now" line stays only for when the core is missing from a build. Add an engine test like crates/emulator-bridge/tests/cboy_frontend.rs that loads a test set through the real entry points. Build it into the .ipa the optional way. Update .kiro/notes/docs/MANIC_PARITY.md's arcade row to say Continuum's own arcade core is in, and what it plays.

items.progress: Konami's sound chip is in (pushed as 3226ddd): cores/continuum-arcade/src/ay8910.rs is the AY-3-8910 with its three tone generators, the 17-bit noise generator, the envelope generator with all 16 shapes, the mixer, fixed or envelope amplitude, the data manual's 16 logarithmic output levels, the register latch with its chip code, the read-back masks and the two I/O ports (through which the Scramble/Frogger boards read the sound command and the timer), ticking at its clock divided by 8 as the chip does. Unit tests prove it against GI's data manual: tone periods 1-4095 and period 0, the noise sequence bit for bit and its 131,071-shift length, all 16 envelope shapes, the envelope step length, the mixer, each channel, the registers, the ports, reset and a save state. It also matches MAME's AY-3-8910 sample for sample (pushed as cb9f2e2): tests/ay8910_mame.rs runs our own Z80 program (tests/ay8910/jumpbug.asm: tones at many periods on each channel, noise at many periods through each channel, all 16 envelope shapes, envelope periods 0-300, periods and shapes changed mid-wave, masked bits, the mixer) on MAME 0.289's Jump Bug board, where the chip's output is exactly 192,000 samples a second, and all 48,715 samples agree with ours (MAME's output-stage voltages taken from a calibration at the start of the script); planted mistakes all fail it. Still to do for I5: the boards themselves (Galaxian, Moon Cresta, Konami's Scramble variant with its sound Z80, the two AY-3-8910s and their filters, and Galaxian's approximated analogue sound).
items.title: The Galaxian board family
items.detail: Namco's Galaxian hardware and its many descendants: Galaxian, Moon Cresta and their clones, and Konami's variant used by Scramble, Super Cobra, Frogger and Amidar, which adds a second Z80 with two AY-3-8910 sound chips. The tilemap, sprites, bullets, the starfield, the colour PROM, the inputs and DIP switches. Galaxian's own sound is analogue circuitry: approximate it from the documented circuit behaviour, and say in .kiro/notes/docs/ARCADE_CORE.md that it is an approximation. Same proof method as I3. Only offer a game once it is proven.
items.progress_board: 16 October: the Galaxian board's picture and timing are done and proven (src/galaxian.rs; ten programs match MAME 0.289 on all 1,800 frames). Galaxian's and Moon Cresta's analogue sound is in (src/galaxian_sound.rs, an approximation, said so in ARCADE_CORE.md; the tone agrees with MAME to 0.2%). Konami's Scramble boards are in and proven (src/galaxian.rs Variant::Konami, src/i8255.rs, src/konami_sound.rs): Scramble, The End, Super Cobra, Frogger and Amidar/Turtles maps; on MAME's scramble, theend, scobra, frogger and amidar sets all 260 frames match pixel for pixel and every sound Z80 instruction matches MAME's trace, the filtered sound within 8% (tests/konami_mame.rs live, tests/konami_board.rs everywhere). Still to do for I5: the set list entries for the Galaxian and Konami boards (scripts/make-set-list.py; per-set inputs and DIP switches, ideally dumped from MAME's port fields with zero-filled stand-in ROMs), recognition in src/sets.rs, Image/Machine in src/board.rs (224 x 768 picture: scale to 3:4 for the app), the DIP switches in src/options.rs, CARCADE_SETS in crates/emulator-bridge/src/import/detect.rs, the refusal sentence, tests/libretro.rs cases; then switch the boards on.

items.progress: The board's sound processor is in (pushed as 9bb5a7e): cores/continuum-arcade/src/mcs48.rs is the Intel 8035/8039 (MCS-48) with every instruction and its machine cycles, both register banks, the stack in RAM, the PSW and flags, F1, the timer and event counter and their interrupt, the external interrupt, P1, P2, the BUS, T0 and T1, MOVX, the 8243 expander instructions and the two program banks (SEL MB0/MB1), with 64 or 128 bytes of RAM. No public per-instruction suite exists for it, so tests/mcs48_opcodes.rs checks all 256 opcodes against Intel's 1980 MCS-48 User's Manual (each instruction written out again from the manual, 768,000 random cases on both RAM sizes, every register, flag, RAM byte, port, timer bit, outside access and cycle count), the opcode table is checked against The Macro Assembler AS, and unit tests cover interrupts, timer, counter, banks, stack, RAM sizes, reset and save states. It also matches MAME's MCS-48 core instruction for instruction (pushed as fb55aa3): tests/mcs48_mame.rs runs four programs of ours (arithmetic over every accumulator value, jumps/banks/stack/PSW, the timer, counter and both interrupts, and the ports, MOVX and BUS as Donkey Kong's board wires them) and all 104,360 instructions agree with MAME 0.289's trace of its Donkey Kong sound board (PC and bank, A, PSW, R0-R7, timer, prescaler, P1, P2 and cycles before every instruction). Still to do for I6: the board itself (the Z80 side, the video, the 8035's wiring to the DAC and the tune ROM, and the approximated analogue sounds).
items.title: The Donkey Kong board
items.detail: Nintendo's Donkey Kong hardware: Donkey Kong and Donkey Kong Jr. A Z80 for the game and an Intel 8035 for the music and sounds feeding a DAC, plus the analogue sound effects (approximated, and said so). Same proof method. Only offer a game once it is proven.

items.title: Write it up
items.detail: Finish .kiro/notes/docs/ARCADE_CORE.md: the games cArcade plays now (set name and title), what each board's tests prove, what is approximate, what is next and in what order (the big ones players want, like Capcom's CPS-1 boards for Street Fighter II and the Neo Geo, need a 68000 processor: say how far away that is), and a short numbered list of phone checks in the owner's plain, casual voice. Then set the top-level complete to true.

notes_14_october: I3 is done (9c39306, a79aa8e): the Pac-Man board matches MAME frame for frame. The chips for I5 and I6 are done and proven: the AY-3-8910 (src/ay8910.rs, sample for sample against MAME) and the Intel 8035 (src/mcs48.rs, instruction for instruction against MAME). Read their 'progress' fields under I5 and I6 first: they carry board wiring notes (Donkey Kong's P2 latch updates at the end of each instruction; the DK program ROM shows in both banks and DK Jr.'s 4 KB program uses both; Konami's boards turn the AY's levels into voltages through their own circuit, so the board models its own output and filters).

The reference MAME (0.289, only the pacman/, galaxian/ and nintendo/dkong.cpp drivers) must be built again in a new sandbox: .kiro/notes/wip/tools/build-mame.sh is the script that built it, and mame-READY.txt beside it says how to run it headless. Build it once, in /projects/sandbox/.scratch/mame, and share it. Never build a second one.

Never edit .github/workflows/ (Kiro's GitHub rules allow no workflow change straight onto master, and the owner allows no pull requests). The two ios.yml lines I4 mentions (the arcade crate's tests in the checks job, cores/continuum-arcade/** in the push paths) are parked: write them, exactly, under a 'Parked' heading in .kiro/notes/docs/ARCADE_CORE.md. Because CI will not run the arcade crate's tests, `cargo test --release` in cores/continuum-arcade must pass locally before every push.

I4: like cBoy, cArcade has no pin, so native/ios/build-engine.sh must drop any cached copy so it is rebuilt on every run (see how cBoy is handled there). In scripts/build-core.sh follow the cache rules added on 14 October (3651403, 1de468f, d8d8654: read 'WHAT COUNTS' above ios_cache_scan and .kiro/notes/docs/reports/cache-v2-verification.md): the IOS_OPTIONAL_CORES entry lands inside the lists region, and the build dispatch can sit in cArcade's own region so adding it rebuilds no other emulator; prove it with `bash scripts/build-core.sh ios-fingerprint <core>` on a few existing cores before and after, and run scripts/check-core-cache.sh.
Order: I4 first (so the proven Pac-Man board reaches players), then I5, I6, I7. Keep .kiro/notes/docs/ARCADE_CORE.md up to date as each lands. Never fetch a commercial ROM.
